summary: Expiry exists only when a client opts in with ttl_seconds, so almost every link lives forever. Add an optional service-level default and make the decided numbers explicit configuration.
root_cause: ShortenerService.shorten only sets expires_at when ttl_seconds is supplied; there is no notion of a default lifetime and the numeric limits are not configurable from the entry point.

impacted.reason: New module-level configuration: default expiry, maximum expiry and whether aliases get the default
Accept an optional default_ttl_s (backward compatible: defaults to None, meaning no default expiry)
Apply the default expiry when no ttl_seconds is given (and the alias rule allows it)
Wire the decided default and maximum into the running service
Reads expiry and returns 410 after it; reviewed, unchanged
Idempotent reuse only matches non-expiring links, so links with a default expiry are never reused; reviewed, unchanged

apis_affected: POST /api/shorten (response now carries an expires_at for links created without ttl)
data_flows: POST /api/shorten -> ShortenerService.shorten -> LinkRepository.add(expires_at) -> GET /{code} -> ShortenerService.resolve -> 410 when expired
data_migration: None. Existing links keep their stored expiry (stated constraint).
risks: Behaviour change: links created from now on expire unless the client asks otherwise (hence the human decision)
Because links with an expiry are never reused, shortening the same URL twice now yields two links under a default expiry
The web UI's 'Never' option now means 'server default'; its label needs a follow-up outside this change
